text: PREFACE SOME FORTY years ago John O’Brien edited a collection of essays entitled The Vanishing Irish:
text_raw:
PREFACE 
SOME FORTY years ago John O’Brien edited a collection of essays 
entitled The Vanishing Irish:

text: The Enigma of the Modern World.
text_raw: The Enigma of the Modern World.

text: O’Brien and the other contributors drew attention to a central fact of Ireland’s modern history: that the island’s population by the mid¬ twentieth century was only about half what it had been prior to the Great Famine.
text_raw:
O’Brien and the other contributors drew attention to a central fact 
of Ireland’s modern history: that the island’s population by the mid¬ 
twentieth century was only about half what it had been prior to the 
Great Famine.

text: This great depopulation reflected not just the deaths and emigration of the Famine years, but a slower and more drawn-out pro¬ cess during the sixty years that followed.
text_raw:
This great depopulation reflected not just the deaths and 
emigration of the Famine years, but a slower and more drawn-out pro¬ 
cess during the sixty years that followed.

text: This book focuses on the popu¬ lation decline of these six decades.
text_raw:
This book focuses on the popu¬ 
lation decline of these six decades.

text: My subtitle, while coupled with O’Brien’s evocative title, signals a basic difference in approach and method.
text_raw:
My subtitle, while coupled with 
O’Brien’s evocative title, signals a basic difference in approach and 
method.

text: I argue that some aspects of Irish depopulation were unusual but that the basic forces leading to depopulation were similar to those at work all across Europe in the late nineteenth century.
text_raw:
I argue that some aspects of Irish depopulation were unusual 
but that the basic forces leading to depopulation were similar to those at 
work all across Europe in the late nineteenth century.

text: Ireland differed from some other places experiencing depopulation primarily in the par¬ ticular combination of demographic forces that brought it about: high emigration rates, large families, and a large number of adults who never married.
text_raw:
Ireland differed 
from some other places experiencing depopulation primarily in the par¬ 
ticular combination of demographic forces that brought it about: high 
emigration rates, large families, and a large number of adults who never 
married.

text: The Irish can be appreciated for the truly unique aspects of their history and culture, but we must remove from the list of things unique to Ireland most aspects of the population patterns that so exercised O’Brien.
text_raw:
The Irish can be appreciated for the truly unique aspects of their 
history and culture, but we must remove from the list of things unique to 
Ireland most aspects of the population patterns that so exercised 
O’Brien.

text: More recent history has also given good reason to rethink the views expressed in the O’Brien volume.
text_raw:
More recent history has also given good reason to rethink the 
views expressed in the O’Brien volume.

text: Irish population growth has been slow and uneven since the 1950s, but there is little danger that the Irish will disappear.
text_raw:
Irish population growth has been 
slow and uneven since the 1950s, but there is little danger that the Irish 
will disappear.

text: Three aspects of this study are paramount.
text_raw: Three aspects of this study are paramount.

text: First, the focus throughout is on rural Ireland.
text_raw:
First, the focus throughout 
is on rural Ireland.

text: The rural focus reflects the fact that Ireland was a very rural country even as late as 1914, and that depopulation was a primarily rural phenomenon.
text_raw:
The rural focus reflects the fact that Ireland was a 
very rural country even as late as 1914, and that depopulation was a 
primarily rural phenomenon.

text: The contribution of urban areas to depop¬ ulation was to grow more slowly than was necessary to offset population decline in the countryside.
text_raw:
The contribution of urban areas to depop¬ 
ulation was to grow more slowly than was necessary to offset population 
decline in the countryside.

text: Second, the focus is on the period between the Great Famine and the First World War, roughly 1850-1914.
text_raw:
Second, the focus is on the period between the 
Great Famine and the First World War, roughly 1850-1914.

text: I stray out¬ side these boundaries only rarely, in search of the historical roots of a post-Famine development or to trace the way a post-Famine develop¬ ment has worked itself out in twentieth-century Ireland.
text_raw:
I stray out¬ 
side these boundaries only rarely, in search of the historical roots of a 
post-Famine development or to trace the way a post-Famine develop¬ 
ment has worked itself out in twentieth-century Ireland.

text: Third, this study aims at once to describe and explain Ireland’s population history and to use that history to illuminate more general population-related phenom¬ ena both in European history and in today’s world.
text_raw:
Third, this study 
aims at once to describe and explain Ireland’s population history and to 
use that history to illuminate more general population-related phenom¬ 
ena both in European history and in today’s world.

text: This broader per¬ spective reflects both my judgment that one cannot understand Ireland in a vacuum and my hope that this small island’s history can offer more

spective reflects both my judgment that one cannot understand Ireland in 
a vacuum and my hope that this small island’s history can offer more

Ireland’s population history poses two serious intellectual challenges: 
why population grew so rapidly prior to the Famine, and why it declined 
for so long after the Famine.

text: This book focuses on why and how Ire¬ land’s population declined during the second half of the nineteenth cen¬ tury.

text: Warren Professor of Demography and Director of the Population Studies Center, University of Pennsylvania “The Vanishing Irish applies a subtle and persuasive blend of economic and institutional analysis to a critical period of Irish demographic history.
text_raw:
Warren Professor of Demography and Director 
of the Population Studies Center, University of Pennsylvania 
“The Vanishing Irish applies a subtle and persuasive blend of economic and 
institutional analysis to a critical period of Irish demographic history.

text: Recogniz¬ ing the uniqueness of Irish institutions but rejecting Irish exceptionalism, Guinnane examines the choices about marriage, childbearing, and emigration made by young Irish men and women between the end of the Famine and the First World War.
text_raw:
Recogniz¬ 
ing the uniqueness of Irish institutions but rejecting Irish exceptionalism, 
Guinnane examines the choices about marriage, childbearing, and emigration 
made by young Irish men and women between the end of the Famine and the 
First World War.

text: The net effect of their choices—late marriage and a high fraction of the population who never married; high levels of marital fertility; and high levels of emigration—was the depopulation of post-Famine rural Ireland and a rapidly aging population.
